title: Contributing: A Codebase Tour
description: Walk through the Pilot Protocol codebase. Architecture, package layout, testing, and how to submit your first pull request.
seoTitle: Contributing: A Codebase Tour | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: You want to contribute to Pilot Protocol. You have cloned the repository, run

, and now you are staring at a tree of packages wondering where to start. This article is the map. It covers the main repositories and packages, explains how the test environment works, walks through adding a new service from scratch, explains the layering rule CI enforces, and suggests where to start.
Pilot Protocol is a pure-Go project: no cgo, no code generation, and
just works. The core module's direct third-party dependencies are few (
lists what they pull in indirectly. The code is split across several repositories under
, each its own Go module, so you can read one part without holding the whole thing in your head.
The daemon and CLI live in
. The registry, the beacon and each daemon plugin are separate repositories that
imports as Go modules. Here is what each piece does and where the important files live.
This is the foundation layer. It defines the 48-bit virtual address format (
), the 34-byte packet header structure, the well-known ports, and CRC32 checksum computation. Nearly every other package imports

. If you are fixing a serialization bug or adding a new message type, this is where you start. The address parsing is strict, and the text format must match exactly. The header includes fields for source/destination addresses, port numbers, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window size, and checksum. All multi-byte fields are big-endian.

The daemon is the heart of Pilot Protocol. It manages the UDP tunnel, handles NAT traversal on the client side, runs the port manager, processes IPC commands from the CLI and SDKs, and coordinates encryption. This is the largest package and the one you will spend the most time reading. Key files handle tunnel read/write loops (

), connection state machines (SYN/ACK/FIN lifecycle) and sliding window transport with congestion control, flow control with advertised receive windows, Nagle-style coalescing of small writes, segmentation (
), keepalive probes, idle timeouts, and graceful shutdown. If you are working on transport reliability, congestion behavior, or connection lifecycle, this is the package.

The registry is the rendezvous server's brain, in its own repository. It handles node registration, address assignment, hostname resolution, networks and their roles and policies, persistence (snapshots plus a write-ahead log), and hot-standby replication. Its
binary runs the registry and a beacon together; use
to set their listen addresses. This binary is what you deploy if you run your own rendezvous. If you are working on discovery, node management, or multi-server coordination, start here.
The beacon handles the server side of NAT traversal. It answers STUN-style discovery requests so daemons learn their external address, coordinates UDP hole-punching (sending
to both peers), and relays traffic when no direct path works. Relayed packets travel in

; the payload stays encrypted end to end. The beacon can listen dual-stack (IPv4 and IPv6). The daemon's fallback chain (direct, hole-punch, relay) spans the daemon and the beacon, so changes here require careful testing across NAT setups.
common/driver - IPC Client and Go SDK
The driver is the Go SDK that applications use to talk to the daemon. It connects over a Unix domain socket (

by default) and provides an API for dialing and listening on ports, sending datagrams, resolving hostnames, and managing trust. It serializes IPC frame writes with a mutex so concurrent goroutines don't interleave frames. The
run over Pilot. If you are building an application on Pilot, the driver is your entry point.
The command-line interface. It wraps the driver with commands like
commands. Most commands are thin wrappers that parse flags, call the driver, and format output (text, or JSON with
). Adding a new CLI command is one of the easiest contributions. Commands like
go through the daemon IPC (not directly to the registry) because the daemon signs them with the node's key.

The test environment is the single most important file for contributors to understand.
creates a miniature Pilot network inside a single Go test process. Here is how to use it:

fields.code:
# Run all integration tests (always use -parallel 4)
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 ./tests/

# Run a specific test
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 -run TestHandshake ./tests/

# Run with verbose output
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 -v -run TestHandshake ./tests/

The daemons communicate over real UDP on localhost, so you are testing the actual network path, not mocks. Test daemons are public, so they can talk without a trust handshake unless the test is about trust.

The project enforces a layered architecture.
assigns every package to a layer (datagram I/O, routing, transport, services, and so on), and imports must always point downward. The
tool reads that file and fails CI on any violation, so if your change adds an import across layers, expect to restructure it rather than suppress the check.

Here is the workflow that regular contributors use:

fields.code:
# Clone and verify the build
git clone https://github.com/pilot-protocol/pilotprotocol.git
cd pilotprotocol
go build ./...

# Run the full test suite
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 ./tests/

# Make your changes, then verify
go vet ./...
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 ./tests/

# Run just the test for your feature
go test -parallel 4 -count=1 -v -run TestYourFeature ./tests/

The codebase is deliberately plain. No frameworks, no generated code, few direct dependencies. Just Go, the standard library, and the problem. Because each piece is its own module with strict layering, you can understand the part you are changing without reading everything else.
